Q: How do dependency inversion and anti-corruption adapters prevent provider details from spreading?
A: Domain code should depend on the behavior it needs, while an adapter translates a provider's transport and data model into that contract. An anti-corruption boundary prevents provider-specific statuses, identifiers and exceptions from silently becoming domain policy. Match semantic guarantees, not just method signatures. Unsupported behavior must remain visible; a wrapper should not claim durable cancellation or tenant isolation that the provider does not supply. Keep the adapter small enough to test against real boundary cases.
Why: A provider's 'accepted' response may mean queued rather than completed. Translating it directly into the domain state 'succeeded' corrupts every caller even though the adapter's return type looks convenient.
Risk: An overgeneric interface can erase distinctions needed for safe recovery.
Trade: Normalize compatible behavior and expose material capability differences explicitly.
Try: Write a contract test distinguishing accepted, completed, denied and unknown outcomes.
